title: The Chief Khalsa Diwan, 1902
hookLine: a central body to coordinate the reform societies

cards: By now the Punjab is full of Singh Sabhas, reform societies in town after town. One runs a school. One prints tracts.
One argues with another about how things should be done. Each is doing good work, and each is doing it alone. Sooner or later someone asks the obvious question: what if we did this together?
The answer was a central council, based in Amritsar, to coordinate the reform: the Chief Khalsa Diwan.

teach.b: First, the name. Diwan is a word for a council or an assembly; Sikhs also use it for a gathering in the gurdwara where hymns are sung. Khalsa is the community of initiated Sikhs.
Chief means it sat above the local societies, a hub for many wheels. Second, what it did.
It brought the Singh Sabhas into one network, so a school in one town and a press in another could share plans, teachers and money.

It started and supported schools, spoke for Sikhs to the government, and worked on causes like the one you'll hear tomorrow. Among its leaders, one name that comes up is Sundar Singh Majithia. Third, the honest part.
Working together isn't the same as agreeing. Some Sikhs felt the Diwan was too cautious with the British, too close to the powerful. Others valued it for getting things done.
Both views are part of the story, and later movements grew partly out of that disagreement.

teach.h: A WEEK OF BUILDERS, ONE SANGAT.
teach.b: Fourth, the week behind it. Kahn Singh, building a treasury of words. Macauliffe, with Sikh scholars checking his six volumes.
Bhai Vir Singh and his heroine, Sundri.

Takht Singh and Harnam Kaur, and their school for girls. Every one of them needed others. The Gurus called the gathering of the faithful the sangat, and in Gurbani the company of the holy is where a person is lifted.
The Diwan was an attempt to turn many good efforts into one sangat.

how: The Chief Khalsa Diwan still exists in Amritsar and runs schools and other institutions; Sikh communities today coordinate their work through gurdwara committees, councils and networks of local sangats.

games.q: you lead one Singh Sabha. other societies are doing similar work, separately, sometimes arguing. what do you do?
o: keep your society independent and ignore the rest.
join a central council to coordinate the work.
close your society and let the others carry on.
games.why: the reformers formed the Chief Khalsa Diwan in Amritsar to coordinate the Singh Sabhas, and disagreements came along too.

practice: Bring to mind something you're doing alone that someone else is also doing alone: a project at work, a family task, a cause you care about.
Picture the two of you comparing notes and dividing the load, not agreeing on everything and still moving forward. If you pray, let Waheguru steady the breath as you hold that picture.

wordCard.voice: Diwan, a council or assembly: the Chief Khalsa Diwan, a central council in Amritsar that drew the Singh Sabha societies into one network, to work together. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: working together. It's slower, and it's how a school in one town could borrow a teacher from another. Day nine hundred seventy-three, and a week of builders behind you.
